title: Non-coding variant effect prediction · Saturday, November 28

transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Non-coding variant effect prediction, for Saturday, November 28.
Let's turn to Non-coding variant effect prediction. One new preprint today, from the Gerstein lab, posted on bioRxiv.

It's called HapAdapter. It starts from a basic limitation: DNA foundation models are trained on the haploid reference genome, so they struggle to use a person's full diploid genome when predicting what a variant does.
So the question is whether you can retrofit a pretrained model to handle both haplotypes. How do the authors do it?

They add a small Siamese adapter head on top of a pretrained model, here DNABERT-2 and AlphaGenome. The adapter takes diploid personal-genome context and predicts allele-specific effects, so the large model itself stays as it is.
And the result, across nine assays, is that it roughly doubled DNABERT-2's above-chance AUROC and roughly tripled AlphaGenome's for telling allele-specific effects apart.
Notice the phrase above chance. That is gain over the 0.5 baseline, so a tripling can still leave a modest absolute AUROC. The summary doesn't give the absolute values.
Good caveat. It's also a preprint, and we don't have the abstract, so we can't say which assays or individuals were used, or how well it generalizes to new people.
Still, a light adapter protocol is a practical way to reuse costly foundation models for personal genomes.

Takeaway: a small diploid-aware adapter clearly improves allele-specific prediction from foundation models, but we need absolute performance numbers and peer review before judging how big the gain really is.

papers.title: HapAdapter: A Transfer Learning Protocol for DNA Foundation Models Adapted to Diploid Personal Epigenomes
